## Short answer

Nobody picked their own moment. Every person in the group let go on one shared, externally
given cue, delivered from off-camera at the photographer's position. The man in ceremonial

is following it, and in fact he does not throw anything at all during the toss. He sits

It is a single continuous take (no cuts anywhere in the 69.6 s — the only apparent changes
of composition are the camera panning and zooming), with **no audio track at all**, so the
cue has to be inferred from bodies and timing rather than heard. The subject is a
convocation group photo: roughly 120 people in black academic gowns, arranged in tiered
rows — seated on chairs at the front, standing behind, more standing on risers at the back
— inside a function hall. At the centre of the front row sits a man in a red-and-gold
ceremonial robe wearing a red bonnet; a second, different man in similar ceremonial dress
stands directly behind him. Everyone faces the camera the entire time.

## The sequence, with timings (25 fps, so one frame = 40 ms)

- **0 – 38.5 s** — the group is already posed and essentially frozen while the camera pans
  and zooms across the arc of people. No caps move.
- **≈ 38.6 – 39.0 s** — the mortarboards come off. This is not a scatter of individual

  centre and right together.
- **39 – 41.4 s** — caps held up and waved in the air.

  0.15 s of one another. Stepping through 42.4 – 44.2 s frame by frame shows this was a
  **rehearsal**: the caps are thrown up, caught again, and put back on or held. So there
  are two coordinated rounds, not one, which by itself rules out individual timing — a
  whole group does not spontaneously rehearse together.
- **≈ 43 – 55.7 s** — a long frozen "ready" hold of roughly 11–13 s. The caps are held
  cocked at shoulder or head height and **not one person releases early**. That is the
  single most decisive piece of evidence: for over ten seconds every one of about 120
  people is visibly waiting for something outside themselves before letting go.
- **55.72 – 55.80 s** — the definitive release. It is confined to two to three frames,
  i.e. roughly 80–120 ms. I checked this at the far left of frame and the far right of
  frame separately, cropping each end and stepping at 25 fps: both ends wind up and let go
  in the same two-to-three-frame window as the centre. The simultaneity is group-wide, not
  just a local cluster copying its neighbours.
- **56.4 – 56.7 s** — the caps land, all of them on the carpet in **front** of the group,
  toward the camera. Everybody threw in the same direction, at the camera, which is where
  the cue came from.
- **57 – 69.6 s** — arms up, a brief cheer, then the group settles straight back into the

  floor in front of them. They hold that arranged pose to the end of the clip instead of
  breaking up, which is what people do when the photographer is still shooting and still in
  charge of the moment.

1. **Spread of release times.** A release spread of two to three frames across roughly 120

   person-to-person chain reaction would show a visible ripple sweeping across the frame.
   There is no ripple; the left edge, the centre and the right edge go together.
2. **A coordinated wind-up, not just a coordinated release.** The arms cock together before

3. **The long frozen hold with zero defectors.** Eleven-plus seconds of everyone holding

7. **The aftermath.** Settling back into the arranged rows and applauding, rather than
   dispersing, shows the group is still being directed.
8. **No flash, no audible signal available.** I measured mean luma frame by frame across the

   so the cue was almost certainly a spoken count ("three, two, one — throw!") from the

The release was a single collective act on one shared cue given from behind the camera by
the photographer running the shoot, evidenced by the coordinated removal wave, the
synchronised rehearsal toss and catch, the eleven-second frozen hold with no early releases,
the two-to-three-frame release window simultaneous at both ends of a 120-person group, the

everyone else.
